utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now, I'm turning to the Defence, who is going to start? Ms. Alaburic?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Each witness will have half an hour. Of course, you can share the time between you if you so wish.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, witness, good afternoon and good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. Witness, I am the Defence counsel for General Milivoj Petkovic in these proceedings, and you're just receiving the documents that I've prepared for my cross-examination. I would like to explain to the Trial Chamber that the orange binder contains the documents that are already exhibits. Witness, in your statements, and in the documents that were attached to the statement, you talked to us about the 9th of May 1993 and the conflicts that started at the time so I'm not going to deal with that at present, but I am going to deal with the attempts made to stop the conflict. So I'd like to start off by asking you to look at my set of documents and particularly documents 4D 00456 and 4D 00457. They are statements by Mr. Mate Boban and Alija Izetbegovic dated the 10th of May 1993, in which they each to their own army issue orders for a cease-fire and authorise the commanders of the armies, Sefer Halilovic and for the HVO Milivoj Petkovic, to meet and try to reach an agreement for a peaceful settlement of the conflict between the two armies and two authorities. Tell me, please, were you aware of these orders? Did you know about them on the 10th of May 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the first time I've seen this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes, I believe you when you say that. But did you know that the presidents, Izetbegovic and Boban, issued orders of that kind or those orders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't know. Perhaps I wasn't high enough ranked to know of this.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now, let us take a look at the following document: P02344, which is an agreement between Halilovic and Petkovic dated the 12th of May 1993, and it is a document which you mention, and which was dealt with by your organisation. Are you familiar with the agreement? If so, we can discuss it. And to start off, in view of your statement on the deployment of a unit of SpaBat in Mostar, and my client intervened, General Petkovic, on that issue, I'd like to ask you the following: Have you ever heard or, rather, did you ever hear of a Spanish Battalion unit which was in Mostar otherwise, on the 9th of May, in the morning, when the attack that we are going to discuss happened, was not in Mostar? Did you ever hear of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The information concerning the 9th of May were very confusing. Our patrol and our units in Mostar were told to leave. Obviously, we left some kind of informer or some kind of -- so that we could get some kind of information concerning the occurrences there, but on the 9th of May we did not have a unit in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in the unit you just mentioned as having been in Mostar. Might it have been a unit which was deployed in Mostar since the 20th of April 1993, on the basis of another agreement that was reached in Mostar at the time, which we won't be discussing now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Mostar, at that time, given our deployment in Mostar, we did not have a unit at that particular time in Mostar. There was a unit previously which was there to protect the convoys passing through. Those convoys were not able to go through on the 9th of May, and we had to leave the area under fire. I do not know which unit you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well, Witness. We're not going to deal with that now. We'll be going into those facts with other witnesses. But take a look at Article 2 of this particular agreement between Halilovic and Petkovic on the 12th of May 1993. And in that Article 2, they have agreed that a company of the Spanish Battalion will be deployed and accommodated in Mostar at the airport until more suitable accommodation can be found, and then they say that the deployment will be on both sides and will begin on -- at 1800 hours on the 12th of May 1993. So was that the deployment of the company you mentioned on the basis of this agreement? Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was the objective, but it wasn't actually carried out within the time frame that was envisaged. There was a deployment in the airport.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, in the night between the 12th and 13th, a SpaBat unit did enter the Mostar area; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just one moment. I wasn't in -- I didn't have the logbook here with me. If I remember right, at the end of the day of the 12th, maybe, but I'm not sure -- yes, yes, given the information I have it was on the 12th itself that there was a deployment of our patrols towards the confrontation line. Yes. And they had contact with the HVO to make sure that -- because it was the HVO who had all the check-points concerning the entry and exit of the city.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's move on to the next article, Witness. I know about the situation in Mostar and it will become even clearer to us during the rest of today and tomorrow, but take a look at the last two sentences in Article 3. This is what it says in that part of the article. In the area of Kostajnica and Konjic, HVO units will be deployed in a few villages in the area marked on the attached map. The BH army will withdraw out of this area to their own villages. Now, I'd like you to explain to us what was going on in the area of Kostajnica and Konjic that was so important for it to be recorded in this agreement and to be treated in exactly the same way as Mostar and the events in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I repeat that in my area of responsibility, for our task force, I didn't have in detail knowledge of the comments, but I do know that in Kostajnica these are two enclaves, Kostajnica and the Konjic pocket, they were controlled by the HVO, who slightly expanded its area of influence. I recognise this document because at our level we didn't have detailed documentation as to the agreement between these two generals. I don't know much more about this, but I remember that the Konjic enclave was of great concern to the Spanish Battalion, and I remember that the importance of this supply route towards this area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Alaburic, just a small question I would like to ask you. We've seen this document 20 or 30 times over. I notice that in Article 3, a map is mentioned. I don't know whether we've seen this map already. Do you have any idea about this? Because it seems that Kostajnica and Konjic are mentioned on this map.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] An attached map was -- is mentioned but the map wasn't attached to this Prosecution document, but I think that my client, General Petkovic, would like to say something in connection with this, so perhaps we should hear what he has to say first. THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, once again a technical matter. The witness must know about the document. Witness, on the 12th of May, were you in Medjugorje when there was a meeting between Petkovic and Malvic and General Morillon and Mr. Thebault?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, I was present, General, but the document, as a head of section, was never shown to me. This is a document which remained at the level of the people who signed it and with the authority that had it drafted. I never had a copy of the reports. I confirm that this is the first time I have seen this document. I don't know if I have answered your question. THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Let's move slowly through this. The agreement signed by UNPROFOR, the UNPROFOR commander, and you were his subordinate, says that a company of the battalion will be deployed in Mostar. Is that what it says in Article 2? A company of yours? And actually you confirmed to my counsel that that is correct, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. This is the text, and in this text it says that there will be a company deployed on the 12th, and I remember that at the end of the 12th of May, there was a Spanish company, but I repeat this is the first time I've seen this text. THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] Your unit in Jablanica was a component part of your battalion; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was part of a task force. I wasn't part of -- I was a member of the staff. The staff of the task force and my responsibility had nothing to do with the deployment of the unit in question but, rather, with the UNPROFOR mission dealing with -- with humanitarian aid and working between the warring parties. The deployment of a SpaBat unit, I did know about, but obviously there were many other elements of the staff involved. I wasn't focused on those issues. It was not my responsibility. THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] Then you don't know that your company from Jablanica was given the assignment of patrolling the Jablanica-Tarcin stretch, Jablanica-Kostajnica as well, that area, and between Ostoza [phoen], Trusina, Seonica and Vrci.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No. I didn't actually say that I didn't know about that. Obviously our unit in Jablanica had responsibilities ensuring the coverage of roads leading to and from Jablanica and one of the areas involved was the Konjic pocket, but my responsibility was not -- was not such that I knew which unit was deployed where, whether -- where the lines were, et cetera. That wasn't my responsibility. THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] Then I don't know what your duty was, what your task was. You were a high UNPROFOR official as far as I'm concerned located in Medjugorje, and you attended all the meetings. Furthermore your command received this document because it was signed by your commander, General Morillon. It must have received it because were you duty-bound to enter Mostar and to patrol Konjic and Jablanica. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Obviously, between the commander, who was writing, and General Morillon, there was other units, and I can't name them all. In the documents, since UNPROFOR had the order to enter into Mostar, I remember -- I remind you, this order did not reach me as a commander of the task force. THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] I'd like you to look at the signatory of this document finally, read the names.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It seems to me that first I can see an error here. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] Witness, I'd like to remind you of paragraph 44 of your statement where you say on the 12th of May, the Spanish Battalion debated how to deploy a company which would control Mostar from Dracevo in the area around the conflict. That's what you say in your statement. So you know what your battalion was doing. So I'm surprised that such a high-ranking officer doesn't know about the implementation of a document like this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The actions of the task force are under orders from the operational sections. We do not get involved in civic or military issues. Obviously the battalion did as ordered, and it was told to go to Mostar. But I'm not the person who gives the order to the battalion. Nor am I the person who receives the agreements such as the one you're talking about. From General Morillon to myself there is a whole chain of command involving more than ten people. THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] Just one more question about the Spanish Battalion. On the 20th of April when General Pellnas asked for your forces in Mostar, did your government agree that those forces should be in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The deployment in April was done to patrol the city of Mostar, and the Spanish government obviously authorised this mission. This mission was not conducted at UNPROFOR's initiative. We must remember that UNPROFOR, as its name suggests, is a protective force of the United Nations. This order turned UNPROFOR into a buffer zone between two warring factions. Officially, they were supposedly allied against a third element. The Spanish government naturally authorised our extended mission or the extension of our mission, or otherwise we would not have had units in Mostar trying to separate these formerly allied groups. That's clear. THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'll now let my Defence counsel carry on.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, I have a question to ask you with respect to Jablanica and Kostajnica. In one of the documents prepared by the Prosecution for your testimony, and that is P02461, you needn't look for it because it doesn't matter, you needn't look at it now, but if Their Honours would like to have a look, then on page 13 of the English text is where they can find it, anyway, the Spanish Battalion recorded that it still does not have access to Kostajnica and then goes on to stay that the Muslim offensive in the area of Jablanica is being continued in the area of Kostajnica and Klis. Now, tell me, please, do you have any knowledge at all about the Muslim offensive in the area of Kostajnica in mid-May 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Spanish task force and UNPROFOR knew of all of the information that was provided to us, no more, no less, and they were being informed. You are reading a page from a SITREP, if I'm not mistaken. I hope you will correct me if I'm wrong, but if you're reading from the SITREP, the information that came which it did not come from me, but I knew of this information, I as a member of staff, read the internal staff documentation. But this does not mean that I had to know all details of what was going on in Konjic or Kostajnica. Remember, I knew what was going on Kostajnica. I knew there was a problem when I heard of the four interpreters that were held there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about the details. What we're interested in is whether you knew at the time about the Muslim offensive which is mentioned in this report. I don't want to ask you the details of it, but from your answer I can conclude that did you know about it, but you didn't know about the details of the offensive. So can you just give me a short answer, just say yes or no, am I right or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you please ask me a question that enables me to answer yes or no? You want to know yes or no that I was aware of what, exactly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm listening very carefully to what you say. You're mentioning a Muslim offensive. Where is it mentioned in document 2461? Which is the sentence stating this?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 13 of the English text, Your Honours. I can't find it now, but I'll do my best to find it together with you. Here it is. Page 13, I've found the text. And this is what it says, Muslim offensive in the Jablanica region [In English] continues to the HVO pockets in the area of Kostajnica, Klis, [Interpretation] Et cetera. So that is the penultimate paragraph on page 13 of the English text, and my question referred to that report by SpaBat.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And the question refers to the obligation taken upon -- that the Spanish Battalion took upon itself to go into Kostajnica in order to protect the Croatian population and that that obligation was not fulfilled. So that is interesting for us in the context of the problem of the implementation of this agreement. So that is the essence of my questions. I've spent quite a lot of time on this. It wasn't my intention to do so, and I hope that the Trial Chamber will give us a little more time to continue discussing the topics we planned to discuss.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can't have more time. Please continue with your questions, with your main questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Witness, do you know that after that 12th of May, Generals Petkovic and Halilovic met on the 13th of May also at the Spanish Battalion headquarters and on the 14th of May in the same place along with the presence of the representatives of international humanitarian organisations and UN observers, and then the following day, on the 15th of May, in the same location, this was a meeting which began late at night and finished in the early hours of the following morning, and on the 18th of May, as well, in Medjugorje, when the meeting between Tudjman, Izetbegovic, and Boban took place and then on the 19th of May as well, also in Medjugorje in the presence of Mr. Morillon and Mr. Prado and on the 20th of May a new meeting, once again with the Spanish Battalion, and then on the 21st of May in Kostajnica, et cetera? Now, do you know that in May, Generals Halilovic and Petkovic spent this much time during that month together trying to find a peaceful solution to the conflict between the HVO and the BH army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course we knew that they were meeting. Every time they met, in our headquarters, and it was my responsibility to follow. We knew where they had the rooms, where they had telephones they might need to use. Body guards, et cetera. It was part of our mission. So yes, we knew. Of course I met -- Generals Petkovic and Halilovic talking together. And sometimes they were talking very heatedly between themselves. And I don't know, obviously, what they were talking about between them, but I can confirm the dates. Some of these dates at least that you have mentioned in Medjugorje. I knew of those ones because I was there at that time. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes. All the dates I mentioned are only based on Spanish Battalion reports. Now I would like to talk about the Heliodrom. You told us, Witness, that there were three visits paid by international organisations to the Heliodrom and that you were at the Heliodrom on the 20th of May. That is to say, on that third visit. Is that right? Did I properly convey your own words?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: On that day, the 20th of May, in the logbook of your unit, what is noted is that General Prado personally visited the refugee camp at the Heliodrom in order to see for himself that prisoners were being released. Tell me, this had to do with Mr. Prado's visit to Heliodrom -- to the Heliodrom and you were in attendance, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It reflects the visit of General Prado's visit, who was the head of the Spanish contingent, to oversee the release of those detained. Personally I was there because I was interested in seeing what it was like because I was very interested in seeing for myself, and we had our discussions with him and with interpreters to -- and I think all of that is reflected in the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, could you kindly give shorter answers because I have very little time available. So can we agree that General Prado went to Heliodrom in order to oversee the release of prisoners? Right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some of the prisoners had already been released. He went to check that that had been done because I had never been in the Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Please have a look at document 4D 00614. In my set of documents, it is underneath the binder, witness, just look at them, on the desk that is in front of you, underneath the binder. This is a document of the Security Services Centre of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the signatory is Mr. Ramo Maslesa. The date is the 29th of May 1993. In the first sentence, it says, "On the 19th of May, all detained civilians were released from the Heliodrom prison." Witness, can you confirm for us whether this is correct, what I just read out to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the first time I've seen this document. I think it goes from the Ministry of the Interior to the International Red Cross. You're talking about this paper here?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, now I'm not asking you about who sent this document to who. I'm asking you whether, according to your information, the first sentence is correct, namely that on the 19th of May, 1993, all detained civilians were released from the Heliodrom prison. Does that correspond to your own knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I was there in the Heliodrom, on the 20th, accompanying General Prado, there were some people, men and women, there in the region, and they -- we were told that these were joint prisoners and they -- there were some cases pending still. The Red Cross was there with us. I'm not saying that on the 20th no one was there. There were people there in the Heliodrom. We saw them. And General Prado had the chance to talk to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you make a distinction between civilians who were detained at the Heliodrom and persons who may have been members of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina or had some other kind of detainee status? Just very briefly, do you make a distinction or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course, I can't certify the difference, but I'm saying that a person who is 60 years old is more likely to be a civilian and a person of military age is more likely to be a soldier. They were dressed in mufti, in just civilian clothes, so I couldn't distinguish. We were shown how there were -- they were introduced to us as shared prisoners or joint prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, in view of the fact that we have the documents of the Spanish Battalion on the release of civilians and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, excuse me, an observation on the transcript. On line 25, we read that they were introduced to us as shared prisoners or joint prisoners. But the prisoners said [Spanish spoken] which means common, normal, and I think it refers to detention on remand but that is a question I could call -- ask.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with you. I hadn't read the translation, and I thank you for that, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, how much time does Ms. Alaburic still have?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour in view of the fact that tomorrow we are going to be working extended hours, and as far as I know we only have this witness envisaged, I suggest that you grant the Defence more time to hear this witness because indeed if we are dealing with a witness statement consisting of 250 paragraphs, half an hour is really nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We do have another witness who is scheduled. We have two witnesses. So today and tomorrow we'll have this one and then comes another one the day after tomorrow. This is the reason why I have to be very strict as to the time you use. You have used so far 24 minutes. You still have another six minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But, Your Honour, as far as I know we are going to be working four days this week and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. He's not the only one. We have another witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, four days, two witnesses. This is the first day of our week, and that means that tomorrow we can be dealing with this witness only. I really do not see why the Defence's cross-examination is being so constrained and perhaps yet again we are going to have a situation where the Prosecutor is going to have more time for his redirect than we will have for our cross-examination. I would like to ask for additional time. As far as I can see things, I haven't even started cross-examining this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, in conclusion, I would just like to refer to all the topics on which I did not manage to cross-examine this witness and then I'll use the rest of my time as best I can. Witness, on the 11th of June 1993 -- well, the Prosecutor showed you this today. In your personal diary you refer to something about detentions of a large number of Muslims, and also you say that you expressed your concern about that to officials of the HVO. Could you please tell us briefly, concisely, and clearly, what kind of detentions were you referring to in June 1993 in this part of your diary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was information, information was received, about the fact that there was a large number of Muslims. We didn't know where they were from at that time, but we knew that they were being held in the Heliodrom area. A colonel told me to express the international -- the UNPROFOR's international concern on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you please tell us in which document of the Spanish Battalion from June 1993 such a detention of Muslims in the Heliodrom is recorded? Can you tell us where this is exactly, in what report? If not, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The information about this mass detention in the Heliodrom, if you want to know -- does the Defence counsel wish to know about that? I don't question the orders I receive. When I received orders from the colonel to go to the HVO authorities and with the information that SpaBat had received to say that this was not acceptable, the international community was not going to accept this mass detention, I don't know where this document is.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, please, please, I am asking you about a document. If you're not aware of a document where such a mass arrival of Muslims in the Heliodrom was recorded, then let's move on. Obviously you cannot either remember now or you do not even know that such a document exists, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know -- I don't know -- I have some feedback problems. I don't know which document you are referring to. I can confirm, however, that I attended a meeting for the head of the task force and every time --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, could you please listen to me? If you do not know about a document that contains a report on something like that, say that you don't know about it, that you received orders to convey such an objection, as a good soldier that you did that, but that you have no idea what the substance of this kind of objection was. I am satisfied with that kind of answer. Is that what actually happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course, I don't know about the existence of a document. What I do know is that when there is an entry in the diary it's because there was some action carried out under orders.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. That's your personal diary. Let's move on. I'm interested in humanitarian aid to Mostar. Tell me, please, is it correct that until the end of June 1993, there were no problems in terms of delivering humanitarian aid either to the east or west part of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until the end of June? Absolutely not. This is not --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would like to -- I would like to remind you that in my diary on the 9th of June, I headed a meeting in Medjugorje with the humanitarian aid organisations in which we expounded numerous problems. The civilian problems in Jamahala [phoen] neighbourhood were -- there were serious problems with the organised force supplying -- we were not provided with the assistance required. On the 9th of June, there was no humanitarian aid in Mostar. You're talking about the end of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, I'm going to tell you exactly what it was that I referred to now. I referred to part of your operations logbook on the 26th of June. That's the date, the 26th of June, where it says that the Spanish Battalion negotiated with the UNHCR about a convoy of humanitarian aid. Also I would like to refer you to document P3371 that we saw a few minutes ago, where it says that on the 10th of July, the Spanish Battalion was waiting for UNHCR convoy at one of the locations within their area of responsibility. That was my question related to humanitarian aid that was delivered without any problems whatsoever until the end of June 1993 in the entire area of Mostar regardless of what bank of the Neretva River one took into consideration. Can you agree with that? Just say yes or no, please, just say yes or a no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now I'm going to read out to you what a witness from the UNHCR said when giving evidence in this courtroom. For the Trial Chamber and for the transcript, the transcript reference is 17219, 17285, and the witness before her on page 7239. Witness, please look at me. You're not going to find this anywhere in your papers. The representatives of the UNHCR said the following: That the UNHCR regularly provided aid to East and West Mostar up until the attack of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina at HVO barracks on the 29th or the 30th of June. Tell me, these lady witnesses from the UNHCR, were they telling the truth or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'd like to know which UNHCR people were in Mostar at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Witness, that the first convoy that did not arrive in Mostar was from the second half of July 1993? Just say whether you know or you do not know? You're not going to find anything in your papers. You're not going to find all answers to the questions put to you in your diaries. Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could tell me the date again, please? The date? Could you repeat the date? Up to when, do you say?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, but I don't have time for you to read your diaries now and to go through all of these dates. Just tell me to the best of your recollection, do you remember that the first convoy that set out to Mostar that was supposed to go to Mostar and that did not arrive in Mostar was a convoy from the second half of July 1993? Just tell me whether you remember or not. Or do you remember that that was not the case, that it was different?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I was trying to be accurate. No, I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Could the interpreters please leave the switch or change the switch when the witness speaks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Alaburic, you have no time left. If we have more time tomorrow, you can have the floor again, but we need to keep up the pace. Otherwise we will overstep the allotted time. So you can continue tomorrow if we have some extra time and you can ask those questions which you were unable to put today, but now we have to move on to the next Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask if I could give an explanation. Do we only have this witness all day tomorrow? Then I will know how much time I could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We only have this witness tomorrow. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we know what time has been given to the Prosecution for redirect? Since the entire Defence has three hours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. This will depend on your questions largely. I don't know. So we will see that tomorrow. Next Defence counsel. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have no questions for this witness, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Ibrisimovic. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, actually we have just a few questions for the witness here today.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at your statement again, the one that you looked at a few moments ago? I'm referring to paragraphs 88, 89 and 90. Mr. Pusic is referred to there. Have you found the paragraphs? You have, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: In this statement, I see that you stated that you never saw Mr. Pusic in military uniform.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I don't think I ever saw that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: I don't think I ever saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: And that you contacted him in relation to prisoner exchanges, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With Berislav Pusic, do you mean, or when we are dealing with people who worked with, yes, we were in contact with him, yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You said today that the exchange of prisoners was not part of your mandate, that you were there to provide services or assistance to the International Red Cross, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. UNPROFOR protected the Red Cross when there was an exchange of prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: I looked at your statement from November and December 1997, so I would like to quote from page 10 in the English version. You said then, "Pusic did not have the last say. He only acted in the field." No, it's not that statement. It's the witness from 1997. And you repeated something along those lines in paragraph 89 in your current statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: M'hm. Yes. Yes, that is correct. In paragraph 89, in my opinion, it seemed that he always had to consult someone else. Obviously, for me, well, that's my interpretation. It could be a strategy to gain time, of course, but it seemed to me that he always acted as though he had to ask someone else first. He never took quick decisions saying, right, okay, this afternoon it will be done. No, there were always delays.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Can we please have a look at this document? I think you've actually seen it already with the Prosecutor. It's document P04870. I think there is something that remained unclear in the transcript. For the transcript, in English, it is page 8 and in Spanish it's page 5. Miscellaneous.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: It says here that the BH commission, the one that probably dealt with exchanges, confirmed that they would not go to the location concerned until a list is received on the basis of which one could act. Is that right? Through Mr. Pusic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is exactly what is reflected.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: And then it says Mr. Pusic sent them a list with which they agreed by telephone, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. What it says in the document is that one side, BiH, said that until it received the document that Mr. Pusic had promised them, they would not go to Jablanica. That's what it says. I hope that the English version says the same thing. This means that UNPROFOR did not have access to those lists. These were lists exchanged between the two sides. On one side had to go to Jablanica, but they said they would not go until Mr. Pusic had handed in the list, and this is reflected in miscellaneous.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: But then, it says here, Mr. Pusic sent them a list of detainees with which they agreed over the telephone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It says that the two sides had reached an agreement by telephone to exchange two lists, and that the list from HVO was never reached the Armija side, and therefore the Armija used that as an argument for not going to the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's go back to one matter relating to your interpreter. You made a correction to the statement that when you mentioned Mr. Pusic earlier on in the context of some mafia, that you heard the interpreters speaking. That's what you said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: And I understood it that that was not your interpretation or your opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I wrote in my report, in my statement, was the feeling expressed by my interpreters. I think it's quite rough, calling someone a mafia member. I don't think it's my place to say that, and I would like to make that clear before this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions, witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you had interpreters from both sides, from the Croatian side and the Muslim side, did you? And both interpreters were saying that or was it one pitched against the other?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Spanish army, when it has interpreters, it always has interpreters from the three sides, Serbs, Croatians and Bosnians. And when we go to certain meetings, we had two nationalities always so that we could also always check any clash in interpretation. This was the general feeling that my interpreters had and that's why I used the expression in question. I'm not saying that they were necessarily Muslim interpreters who had that feeling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But after that, was this confirmed, the fact that Mr. Pusic was a mafiosi or was this not confirmed in any way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was surprising for me, Your Honour, that when we tried to do something, we always found a lot of delay in terms of his actions. I interpreted that that he had to check the procedures or perhaps with other authorities. My interpreters weren't giving a clear -- weren't that generous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As we have a few minutes left and there is no point in giving the floor to any Defence counsel, this can be done tomorrow, I would just like to ask you a question which is related to a question that was asked a while ago. But perhaps Mr. Ibrisimovic would like to add something. Would you like to ask a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Microphone not activated] No, Mr. President, I didn't wish to ask anything after your questions. I just want to say that the time left for me I cede to Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. (redacted), could you please look at document 2108, which is a SpaBat diary on the 20th of May? Could you look at the Spanish version, please? This addresses the visit of Mr. Prado to the Heliodrom. Mrs. Alaburic had put you the question, and I wanted to ask you this question: When I read what you wrote down here in Spanish, you mentioned this, General Prado personally visited the refugee camps. He doesn't talk about prisoners. He talks about refugee camps at the Heliodrom, to obtain the release of all the people present there. Why was this camp coined refugee camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Reading this, this was written in the evening of 20th of May, as was usually the case for the official diaries of the battalion, and maybe that's rather a pity. It's talking about the Heliodrom and what you said, you mentioned the specific mission which was Prado's visit to the Heliodrom to ensure the release of prisoners in accordance with the agreements. But for us, it was not a refugee camp. It was a prisoner camp. You are exactly right in pointing that out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. In this document, which is dated, was -- is it generally speaking a duty officer who writes all this down according to the telephone calls or to the information he has, writes everything down and all the information that reaches him in real time? Is that how it happens.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right. It is written when the mission is over, someone comes back from the mission and writes down a very brief summary of what had happened on that mission, and then there were other documents afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And when you draft your report, this is document 10269, did you draft this report on the basis of this document, 2108, or is it that everything you talk about comes from another source?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in my personal summary, I wrote down things that I thought were most important and relevant. Those items weren't always reflected in the logbook. In the logbook there are many more elements than in my personal diary because they reflect the activities of an official nature in our section. In this respect, perhaps I should clarify that initially we didn't have this -- the fifth section logbook, and so I thought it was very important to have this small summary because the documents of this section, the written documents which are sometimes very long and lengthy to work through, so I thought it would be useful to write down when, with whom, and how we had meetings. But in reality, this is part of the task force's history and this is reflected in many other documents, as you already mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you for this clarification. We shall adjourn now. It is very nearly 7.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: (redacted). Witness, as I have told you, you must not discuss any of this with anyone. We shall reconvene tomorrow at 2.15, and if I count the time that's left, there is still Mr. Prlic, Mr. Praljak, and Mr. Stojic who is going to be asking questions. Mrs. Alaburic might take the floor again if we have some time left. Hopefully we will. So much by way of a conclusion. And I'm just waiting for the registrar to give me this order. Mrs. Nozica?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do apologise for taking the floor after you, but I'm not quite clear whether we are here in the courtroom at 2.15 tomorrow or 9.00 tomorrow morning because we were informed that we would be starting at 9.00, so I'd like us to have that cleared up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I thought we were perhaps sitting in the afternoon but if the courtroom is free, then we will start at 9.00. The legal officer has just told me that we are starting at 9.00. We shall therefore be sitting from 9.00 to 12.30 --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, but we work until 5.00 in the afternoon tomorrow, and the day after with a lunch break of about two hours between 12.30 and 2.30.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me repeat. I wasn't properly interpreted. From 9 in the morning until 5 in the afternoon with a lunch break of two hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Very well, that's quite right. Witness, you will therefore come back at 9.00 tomorrow morning and not at 4.15 [sic] As I had said because everybody would be waiting for you which would be a real disaster. So please come back tomorrow morning at 9.00 and we will be able to sit in this courtroom again tomorrow morning. So see you at 9.00 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
